::: {.why}
Capacity is not a property of a signal, it is a property of a signal at a size in a universe with a cost model, and being precise about that is what separates an estimate from a number you made up.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Relate signal autocorrelation to turnover and derive the turnover of a signal from its persistence.
- Estimate the capacity of each signal in dollars, stating the three assumptions that estimate depends on.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>60 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Derive the link: a signal with lag-one autocorrelation rho implies a turnover roughly proportional to one minus rho, and check the relationship against your measured turnover for all four signals. Where it fails, the cause is usually the transform rather than the signal.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [35 min]{.task-min} Estimate capacity: for each signal, find the portfolio size at which the impact cost from qlib/costs.py reduces net information ratio to half its small-size value. Report the number in dollars with the three assumptions attached, which are the impact coefficient, the participation rate you allow, and the universe's dollar volume.
:::
:::

- [Amihud (2002) — Illiquidity and stock returns](https://www.cis.upenn.edu/~mkearns/finread/amihud.pdf) [paper]{.res-kind}

## Deliverable

::: {.deliverable}
Capacity estimates in dollars for four signals, each with the impact coefficient, participation cap and volume assumption stated.
:::

## Checkpoint

::: {.checkpoint}
What is the capacity of your momentum signal, and why is that not a property of the signal alone?
:::
